title: Origin of life
summary: Life on Earth arose from non-living chemistry at an unknown time between about 4.5 and 3.5 billion years ago; the oldest evidence most scientists accept is 3.43–3.48-billion-year-old microbial structures in Western Australia's Pilbara.
card: No one knows exactly when or where living cells first appeared, but the window is bounded by the Moon-forming impact about 4.5 billion years ago and by fossil microbial mats in the Pilbara of Western Australia about 3.48 to 3.43 billion years old. Older claims from Greenland, Quebec and a single Australian zircon, reaching back to 4.1 billion years, remain disputed. Gene-based molecular clocks place the common ancestor of all living things near 4.2 billion years ago, which would push the origin earlier still.
what:
The origin of life is the transition, sometime in Earth's first billion years, from prebiotic chemistry to self-sustaining, evolving cells. It left no direct record, so its timing is bracketed by indirect evidence. The upper limit is set by the giant impact that formed the Moon about 4.51 billion years ago, which would have sterilized the young planet. The lower limit comes from the oldest traces of life that most researchers accept. In the Strelley Pool Chert of the Pilbara Craton, Western Australia, a fossil reef roughly 3.43 billion years old contains seven distinct stromatolite forms whose variety and links to their environment point to microbial builders. The slightly older Dresser Formation nearby, about 3.48 billion years old, preserves stromatolites, organic matter and hot-spring deposits that suggest microbes lived even on land.

Older claims are vigorously disputed. In 2016 a team described 1–4 cm cone-shaped stromatolites in 3.7-billion-year-old rocks at Isua, southwest Greenland; in 2018 another team argued from three-dimensional shape, orientation and chemistry that they are deformation features formed after burial. Haematite tubes and filaments in vent rocks of the Nuvvuagittuq belt, Quebec, at least 3.77 and possibly 4.28 billion years old, have been interpreted as microfossils, though their authors concede abiotic mineral growth cannot be fully excluded and the belt's age is itself debated. Graphite with an isotopically light, life-like carbon signature sits sealed inside a 4.10-billion-year-old zircon from the Jack Hills, Western Australia, but it is one grain and non-biological origins are possible. Independently, molecular-clock studies of gene families date the last universal common ancestor of all cells to about 4.2 billion years ago (4.09–4.33), implying an origin within a few hundred million years of the Moon-forming impact. Sources therefore disagree by more than 600 million years on when life is first securely recorded, because they weigh ambiguous chemical and structural traces differently. Where it began is equally open: submarine hydrothermal vents and volcanic hot springs on land are the two leading candidate settings.

uncertainty.note: This is a window, not a dated event. Start = the Moon-forming impact (~4,510 Ma), used by Moody et al. (2024) as the maximum age for life; the actual origin could fall anywhere after it. End = the oldest evidence of life most researchers accept: Dresser Formation c. 3,480 Ma, or Strelley Pool c. 3,430 Ma if only that reef is accepted (end_plus 50 Myr). If disputed claims are accepted, life is recorded earlier: Isua ~3,700 Ma, Nuvvuagittuq ≥3,770 Ma (possibly 4,280 Ma), Jack Hills graphite 4,100 Ma (end_minus 620 Myr). The record id keeps the queue's -3700my label, which corresponds to the contested Isua claim, not to a consensus date.

how: The steps from chemistry to cells are not directly preserved and remain hypotheses tested in laboratories. In one family of scenarios, life began at alkaline hydrothermal vents on the sea floor, where mineral surfaces and chemical gradients could drive carbon fixation; the inferred metabolism of the last universal common ancestor, an anaerobe using the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway to fix carbon, is consistent with a hydrogen-rich setting of this kind. A rival scenario places it in volcanic hot-spring pools on land, where repeated wetting and drying concentrates organic monomers, links them into polymers, and wraps them in lipid membranes as protocells; the 3.48-billion-year-old Dresser Formation hot-spring deposits are cited as a plausible ancient example. Either way, the sequence must have produced self-replicating molecules, membranes and energy metabolism, and then a population of cells from which all modern life descends. Evidence for the result is read in three ways: fossil structures such as stromatolites built by microbial mats; microfossil-like filaments; and carbon depleted in carbon-13, a signature of enzymatic carbon fixation that can, however, also arise without life. Ancient rocks are metamorphosed and deformed, which is why claims older than about 3.5 billion years are hard to confirm.
why_it_matters: Every organism that has ever lived, from the first microbial mats to the Cambrian animals, dinosaurs and humans, descends from the cells that emerged in this process, so it is the precondition for every other record in the life and human layers of the Atlas. Its direct consequences reshaped the planet itself: by about 3.4 billion years ago microbial communities were building reefs across a shallow carbonate platform, and their descendants went on to evolve oxygen-producing photosynthesis, which transformed the atmosphere and oceans. Had life not arisen, Earth's surface chemistry would have been governed by geology alone, with no oxygen-rich air, no biologically built limestones or soils, and no fossil fuels. The question of how early life appeared also matters beyond Earth. If molecular clocks are right that a complex common ancestor already existed about 4.2 billion years ago, life arose within a few hundred million years of the planet becoming habitable, which suggests that it may emerge readily wherever conditions allow. If instead only the Pilbara evidence stands, the window is longer and the case for quick emergence weaker. That uncertainty shapes the search for life on Mars: the Pilbara and Isua debates are used by NASA and others as test cases for telling genuine biosignatures from mineral look-alikes in rocks of similar age, including the samples collected by the Perseverance rover in Jezero Crater.

related.because: Earth's accretion and the cooling of its surface after the Moon-forming impact produced the oceans, rock surfaces and chemical gradients in which life could arise.
The Cambrian animal radiation was built on about three billion years of evolution by descendants of the first cells, which supplied the genetic and metabolic toolkit animals inherited.

perspectives.holder: Conservative reading of the rock record (e.g. Allwood et al. 2006; Djokic et al. 2017; Duda et al. 2016)
perspectives.account: The oldest evidence that withstands scrutiny is in the Pilbara Craton: the c. 3.43 Ga Strelley Pool stromatolite reef, whose seven forms and environmental patterns argue for microbial builders, and the c. 3.48 Ga Dresser Formation with stromatolites, organic matter and hot-spring textures. Life was certainly present by about 3.5 Ga.

perspectives.holder: Nutman, Bennett, Friend, Van Kranendonk and colleagues (2016)
perspectives.account: Conical and domical structures 1–4 cm high in 3.7 Ga Isua metacarbonates are stromatolites formed in shallow seawater, pushing the fossil record back about 220 million years and implying that life emerged rapidly, in the Hadean.

Three-dimensional shape, orientation relative to the rock fabric, and element chemistry show the Isua structures are deformation features formed long after burial, not stromatolites; the case is a caution for life detection on Mars.

Haematite tubes and filaments in Nuvvuagittuq vent-related jasper, at least 3.77 and possibly 4.28 Ga, are best explained as remains of iron-oxidizing microbes, though the authors concede abiotic chemical gardens cannot be fully excluded. The belt's maximum age is itself disputed: the Québec lexicon treats a 4,321 Ma Sm-Nd age as controversial, against U-Pb zircon ages near 3.78–3.82 Ga.

perspectives.holder: Bell, Boehnke, Harrison and Mao (2015), with commentary by House (2015)
perspectives.account: Graphite sealed in a 4.10 Ga Jack Hills zircon has a carbon-13-depleted signature (−24 ± 5‰) consistent with biology, so a biosphere may have existed 300 million years earlier than thought; the commentary stresses that it is a single grain and that a non-biological, isotopically light carbon source cannot be ruled out.

Dating ancient gene duplications places the last universal common ancestor at about 4.2 Ga (4.09–4.33), already an anaerobic acetogen whose genome encoded roughly 2,600 proteins, living in an established ecosystem, so life's origin must have followed the Moon-forming impact within a few hundred million years. These are model estimates sensitive to calibration.

perspectives.holder: Setting debate: land hot springs (Damer & Deamer 2020) versus submarine hydrothermal vents
perspectives.account: Hot-spring advocates argue that wet-dry cycling in freshwater volcanic pools concentrates and polymerizes organic molecules and that seawater hinders membrane assembly; vent advocates place origins at alkaline sea-floor vents with natural chemical gradients. Neither is established.
